method: warm = median of 7 CLI runs; cold = purge plus 24 GB memory pressure before every query, 3 samples, run as root through osascript

pruning.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the 600M lattice-sorted table: the B0 scan is zonemap-pruned and does not read the whole table

notes: The cold-cache experiment refutes the I/O-dominance hypothesis for the point query on the lattice-sorted table: the B0 scan is zonemap-pruned to 2 of 4,876 row groups, so its cold read is about 19 MB of row-group metadata plus 1 MB of data, not the whole 2.56 GB file. The cold P3 ratio at 600M is 2.7x against 16x warm on the same CLI timer.

The lattice pays a fixed cold-start I/O latency of about 9 to 10 ms (catalog, table metadata, addressed pages), independent of the table size: the 9.9M and the 600M tables both measure 9 to 10 ms cold for the lattice point query.
The scan cold cost grows with N through the row-group metadata traversal (about 0.76 us per row group): 12 ms at 9.9M (81 row groups) against 27 ms at 600M (4,876 row groups).

The B0 scan in the A/B scaling law is therefore a pruned scan, not a full table scan. The full scan (9,938,375 rows, 1 matched) was measured on the random-order gate table. The lattice win is skipping the O(N/122,880) row-group zonemap traversal plus the residual row-group reads; the scaling law holds, but the mechanism differs from the full-row reading.
Wide queries lose in cold as in warm: the S1 lattice at 600M measures 873 ms against 26 ms for the scan.

The I/O-dominance claim would need a workload where the scan reads the whole file: an unprunable layout (random order, incompatible with the lattice closed form) or a query covering nearly all row groups.
A purge-only run without the memory pressure gave similar numbers (partial eviction: 24 ms against 9 ms for the 600M P3), and the pressure protocol is the definitive one.
